original_question: Show that a typical L2 geodesic in D_mu^s(M) has absolute complexity growing linearly in time.
target_in_paper: Problem 21 in Section 8.1 ("Complexity growth for 2D flows"): show that for a typical geodesic γ(t) in D^s_μ(M), one has C(γ(t)) ≃ t.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s actual target: it is about L^2 geodesics in D^s_μ(M), the absolute complexity C(γ(t)), and the claim that for a typical geodesic this complexity should grow linearly in time. This matches Problem 21 in Section 8.1 very closely.
missing_details: The ambient manifold M must be specified: in this problem M is a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary.
D^s_μ(M) should be identified as the Sobolev H^s completion of the group D_μ(M) of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M.
The Sobolev index restriction is implicit in the paper but needed for a stand-alone statement: s > n/2 + 1, hence s > 2 in the two-dimensional setting used here.
The geodesics are geodesics of Arnold’s right-invariant L^2 metric on D^s_μ(M), not geodesics for some other metric.

The notion of absolute complexity must be defined: for ε > 0, one sets B_ε = {v in T_e D^s_μ(M) : ||v||_{H^s} < ε}, U_ε = exp_e(B_ε), and C_ε(η) is the minimal number of factors in a decomposition η = η_1 ∘ ... ∘ η_N with each η_i in U_ε.
The absolute complexity itself must be stated: C(η) = lim sup as ε -> 0 of ε C_ε(η).
The geodesics relevant to the paper’s notion of typicality are geodesics starting from the identity e in D^s_μ(M).

The paper only gives a rough definition of typicality; for a stand-alone formulation one should say that the corresponding set of initial velocities v_0 in T_e D^s_μ(M) has complement of infinite codimension.

The paper writes C(γ(t)) ≃ t but does not spell out the comparison notation there; a self-contained version should say whether this means two-sided linear bounds up to multiplicative constants for sufficiently large t.
If one wants the time-asymptotic reading to be explicit, the question should state that the comparison is intended as t -> infinity.
refined_question: Let M be a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let D^s_μ(M) be the Sobolev H^s completion of the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M, with s > 2, equipped with Arnold’s right-invariant L^2 metric. Let exp_e : T_e D^s_μ(M) -> D^s_μ(M) be the corresponding Riemannian exponential map. For ε > 0, define B_ε = {v in T_e D^s_μ(M) : ||v||_{H^s} < ε}, U_ε = exp_e(B_ε), let C_ε(η) be the minimal N such that η = η_1 ∘ ... ∘ η_N with each η_i in U_ε, and define the absolute complexity of η by C(η) = lim sup as ε -> 0 of ε C_ε(η). Show that for a typical L^2 geodesic γ(t) starting from the identity e in D^s_μ(M)—where typical means that the complement of the corresponding set of initial velocities in T_e D^s_μ(M) has infinite codimension—we have linear complexity growth, i.e. C(γ(t)) ≃ t as t -> infinity (equivalently, up to multiplicative constants, C(γ(t)) grows linearly in t).
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 21 in Section 8.1 almost verbatim. The exact official statement on page 19 is: show that for a typical geodesic γ(t) in D^s_μ(M), one has C(γ(t)) ≃ t. The immediately preceding paragraph in Section 8.1 defines the absolute complexity C via C_ε and the neighborhoods U_ε obtained from the L^2 exponential map, so those definitions are essential to make the question stand-alone. The same subsection also explains, immediately after Problem 21, that typicality is meant in terms of geodesics starting from the identity and initial velocities whose complement has infinite codimension. To make the refined question complete, one must also import from Section 5.2 the definition of the exponential map exp_e on D^s_μ(M) and the Sobolev threshold s > n/2 + 1, and from the introduction the fact that the metric is the right-invariant L^2 metric on the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group. I did not broaden the problem beyond Problem 21, and I did not replace it by the neighboring upper-bound problem (Problem 20).
